Transistor Amplifiers

Learn how a transistor uses DC-supply energy to produce an amplified signal, why a Q-point is necessary, and how nonlinear devices become manageable linear circuits through small-signal models.

9Instructional topics
8PDF figures embedded
8Guided walkthroughs

Learning sequence

  • Amplification and controlled DC power
  • Q-point and signal headroom
  • DC plus small-signal decomposition
  • Tangent-line linearization
  • MOSFET and BJT equivalent models
  • Three amplifier configurations
  • Bias and single-stage design
Begin here · no amplifier background assumed

What “amplification” actually means

An amplifier does not manufacture energy and the input signal does not directly power the load. Instead, the input controls a transistor, and the transistor controls energy delivered from a DC supply.

Voltage gain

\[A_v=\frac{v_o}{v_i}\]

Describes how the signal voltage changes from input to output.

Current gain

\[A_i=\frac{i_o}{i_i}\]

Describes how much output current is produced for a given input current.

Power gain

\[G_P=\frac{P_o}{P_i}\]

The added signal power comes from the DC supply.

Four layers of every transistor-amplifier problem

DC bias: establish a Q-point in the intended region.
Device linearization: calculate \(g_m\), \(r_\pi\), \(r_o\), or \(1/g_m\).
Small-signal circuit: replace the transistor and set DC sources to AC ground.
Performance: find gain, input resistance, output resistance, phase, swing, and distortion.

Two meanings of “saturation”

A MOSFET is normally used as an amplifier in its saturation region. A BJT is normally used as an amplifier in its forward-active region; BJT saturation is a limiting switch region.

Module learning objectives

After completing the module, students should be able to:

1

4

5

Topic 7.1

Basic Principles of Transistor Amplifiers

Signal-controlled use of DC power and the role of the Q-point.

Section introduction

A resistor converts transistor-current changes into output-voltage changes

In the common-source and common-emitter examples, increasing input voltage increases transistor current. The larger current creates a larger drop across the drain or collector resistor, so the output voltage decreases. This explains both amplification and the 180° phase inversion.

Expanded beginner theory

Amplification as a chain of cause and effect

\[ \text{small input voltage} \longrightarrow \text{transistor-current change} \longrightarrow \text{resistor voltage change} \longrightarrow \text{larger output-voltage change} \]

MOSFET common-source

Increasing \(v_{GS}\) increases \(i_D\). Since \(v_o=V_{DD}-i_D R_D\), the output decreases.

BJT common-emitter

Increasing \(v_{BE}\) increases \(i_C\). Since \(v_o=V_{CC}-i_C R_C\), the output decreases.

What is the Q-point?

The quiescent point is the DC operating condition with no time-varying signal. It specifies transistor current and terminal voltages. The signal makes the instantaneous operating point move around this DC value.

\[ \text{MOSFET Q-point: }(V_{GS,Q},I_{D,Q},V_{DS,Q}) \] \[ \text{BJT Q-point: }(V_{BE,Q},I_{C,Q},V_{CE,Q}) \]

Why center placement matters

  • Too close to cutoff: the transistor turns off during one signal half-cycle.
  • Too close to MOSFET triode or BJT saturation: the output cannot continue moving downward linearly.
  • Well inside the useful region: positive and negative signal swings are both possible.

Local voltage gain is a slope

On a transfer characteristic, the small-signal voltage gain is the slope at the Q-point: \(A_v\approx(dv_o/dv_i)_Q\). A negative slope means phase inversion.

Topic 7.2.1

From DC Bias to Small-Signal Operation

Total instantaneous quantity = DC value + time-varying increment.

Section introduction

Uppercase and lowercase symbols describe two simultaneous layers

The transistor does not alternate between “DC mode” and “AC mode.” The DC operating point and the signal variation exist at the same time. Uppercase symbols denote the Q-point; lowercase symbols denote incremental changes around it.

Source-derived notation with beginner expansion

Write every total voltage and current as a sum

BJT examples

\[ v_{BE}(t)=V_{BE}+v_{be}(t) \] \[ i_C(t)=I_C+i_c(t) \] \[ v_{CE}(t)=V_{CE}+v_{ce}(t) \]

MOSFET examples

\[ v_{GS}(t)=V_{GS}+v_{gs}(t) \] \[ i_D(t)=I_D+i_d(t) \] \[ v_{DS}(t)=V_{DS}+v_{ds}(t) \]

What happens to DC sources in the small-signal circuit?

  • An ideal DC voltage source has zero small-signal voltage, so it becomes AC ground.
  • An ideal DC current source has zero small-signal current, so it becomes an open circuit.
  • Coupling and bypass capacitors are often treated as shorts only in a specified midband frequency range.
  • Bias resistors remain and may load the signal source.

Do not add DC and AC circuit equations indiscriminately

First solve the DC circuit to find the Q-point. Then construct a separate small-signal circuit. The two solutions are combined only at the end to recover total instantaneous quantities.

Figure 7.3. Separation into DC and small-signal components

Topic 7.2.2

Meaning of “Small Signal” and Linearization

Approximate a nonlinear curve by its tangent near the Q-point.

Section introduction

Small means small relative to the curvature scale

A signal is “small” when the transistor remains close enough to the Q-point that the local slope is nearly constant. The acceptable amplitude depends on device type, bias point, and distortion requirement.

Expanded mathematical foundation

The first-order Taylor approximation

For an output current \(I=f(V)\), expand around \(V_Q\):

\[ f(V_Q+v) = f(V_Q) + \left.\frac{df}{dV}\right|_Q v + \frac{1}{2}\left.\frac{d^2f}{dV^2}\right|_Qv^2+\cdots \]

The small-signal model keeps only the first-order term:

\[ i\approx g_m v,\qquad g_m=\left.\frac{dI}{dV}\right|_Q. \]

MOSFET saturation

\[ I_D=\frac{1}{2}kV_{OV}^2,\qquad g_m=kV_{OV}=\frac{2I_D}{V_{OV}} \]

BJT active region

\[ I_C=I_Se^{V_{BE}/V_T},\qquad g_m=\frac{I_C}{V_T} \]

Large input creates distortion before obvious clipping

The exact positive and negative current changes are unequal on a curved characteristic. This asymmetry creates harmonics even if the waveform does not yet touch cutoff or another region boundary.

Topic 7.2.3 and Figures 7.5-7.6

MOSFET Small-Signal Models

Controlled current source, finite output resistance, and T-model.

Section introduction

The gate controls current without ideally drawing current

The basic low-frequency MOSFET model contains a dependent current source \(g_m v_{gs}\). Channel-length modulation adds \(r_o\). The T-model is equivalent but places \(1/g_m\) in a source-related branch, which is often convenient for source followers and degeneration.

Detailed model-conversion guide

From the DC transistor to its AC equivalent

Solve the DC circuit and verify MOSFET saturation.
Calculate \(g_m=2I_D/V_{OV}\) and, when needed, \(r_o=1/(\lambda I_D)\).
Replace the transistor by \(g_m v_{gs}\) from drain to source and optional \(r_o\) from drain to source.
Set the DC supply to AC ground and retain signal-source, bias, drain, source, and load resistances.
Use ordinary linear-circuit analysis to find gain and terminal resistances.

Basic parameters

\[ g_m=\frac{2I_D}{V_{OV}},\qquad r_o=\frac{1}{\lambda I_D} \]

T-model relation

\[ r_s^\ast=\frac{1}{g_m} \]

This is an equivalent small-signal quantity, not a physical source resistor.

Ideal infinite input resistance is a low-frequency approximation

The insulated gate draws negligible DC current, but real MOSFETs have gate capacitances that matter at higher frequencies.

Topic 7.2.4 and Figures 7.7-7.8

BJT Hybrid-\(\pi\) and T-Models

Two equivalent ways to represent the same local transistor behavior.

Section introduction

The hybrid-\(\pi\) model emphasizes base voltage; the T-model emphasizes emitter current

Both models describe the same Q-point. Choose the form that makes the external circuit easiest: hybrid-\(\pi\) is often natural for base-driven circuits, while the T-model is convenient for emitter degeneration and emitter followers.

Detailed equivalence guide

Parameters and identities

Transconductance

\[g_m=\frac{I_C}{V_T}\]

Hybrid-\(\pi\) input resistance

\[r_\pi=\frac{\beta}{g_m}=\frac{\beta V_T}{I_C}\]

T-model emitter resistance

\[r_e=\frac{1}{g_m}\approx\frac{V_T}{I_E}\]

Early-effect output resistance

\[r_o=\frac{V_A}{I_C}\]

Why the controlled-source forms are equivalent

\[ g_m v_{be} = g_m(i_b r_\pi) = g_m i_b\frac{\beta}{g_m} = \beta i_b \]

\(r_\pi\) is not the complete amplifier input resistance

Bias resistors and emitter degeneration also affect the resistance seen by the source. The transistor-only \(r_\pi\) is one part of the complete input network.

Supplemental beginner extension aligned with MLO3

The Three Basic Single-Transistor Configurations

Compare common-source/emitter, follower, and common-gate/base stages.

Extension beyond the detailed PDF pages

“Common” identifies the terminal shared by the input and output circuits

The uploaded PDF announces comparison of the three basic configurations but its provided pages primarily develop principles and device models. This section adds the configuration comparison needed for beginner-level circuit analysis.

Configuration map

MOSFET and BJT names follow the same structure

FunctionMOSFETBJTVoltage phaseTypical use
High voltage gainCommon-sourceCommon-emitterInvertingVoltage amplifier
Buffer/followerCommon-drain (source follower)Common-collector (emitter follower)NoninvertingImpedance transformation
Low input resistance / widebandCommon-gateCommon-baseNoninvertingCurrent input, cascode, RF

Common-source/emitter

Large voltage gain, phase inversion, moderate/high input resistance, moderate/high output resistance.

Follower

Voltage gain below but near one, no inversion, high input resistance, low output resistance.

Common-gate/base

Positive voltage gain, low input resistance, high output resistance, useful for current-input or wideband stages.

Degeneration trades gain for stability

An unbypassed source or emitter resistor introduces local negative feedback. It reduces gain magnitude, improves linearity, raises input resistance for a BJT common-emitter stage, and makes performance less sensitive to device parameters.

Supplemental beginner extension aligned with MLO4

Biasing, Headroom, and Clipping

Choose the Q-point before calculating small-signal gain.

Extension beyond the detailed PDF pages

Bias determines the maximum signal swing and whether the model remains valid

Even a stage with high calculated gain is not useful if the Q-point leaves no room for the output to move. The available positive and negative swings are generally unequal, and the smaller headroom sets the maximum undistorted sinusoidal amplitude.

Bias-design workflow

Choose a Q-point systematically

Identify the upper output limit, usually the positive supply.
Identify the lower limit: MOSFET saturation boundary or BJT \(V_{CE(sat)}\).
Place the Q output near the midpoint between the limits for approximately symmetric swing.
Use the resistor drop to determine the Q current.
Calculate the required input bias and verify the transistor region.
\[ V_{o,Q,\text{center}} \approx \frac{V_{\max}+V_{\min}}{2}, \qquad \hat v_{o,\max} = \min(V_{\max}-V_{o,Q},V_{o,Q}-V_{\min}) \]

Clipping is not the only source of distortion

A signal can remain between the output limits and still be distorted because the transistor characteristic is curved. Small-signal validity and large-signal headroom are separate checks.

Choose a Q-point and prove that the desired output swing fits

Treat large-signal headroom and small-signal linearity as two separate checks.

Integrated design walkthrough

Single-Stage Amplifier Design Walkthrough

Combine Q-point, transconductance, loading, degeneration, and input attenuation.

Cumulative engineering walkthrough

The device gain is not necessarily the source-to-load gain

Signal-source resistance, bias-network loading, output loading, degeneration, and finite output resistance all reduce or modify the gain predicted by the simplest formula.

Step-by-step complete-stage analysis

Analyze from the source to the load

Find the transistor small-signal parameters from the DC Q-point.
Find amplifier input resistance, including bias resistors and transistor input resistance.
Use a voltage divider with source resistance to find the actual transistor input signal.
Combine drain/collector resistance, transistor \(r_o\), and load resistance.
Apply the intrinsic stage-gain expression, including degeneration.
Multiply input attenuation by stage gain to obtain overall source-to-load gain.

Analyze a complete single-stage amplifier from source to load

Use one consistent sequence so source loading, device gain, output loading, and headroom are not mixed up.
